en: A natural liking for or attraction to someone or something; a close similarity
hook: AFFINITY: a magnet with INFINITE attraction.
story: Affinity. A natural liking for someone or something; also, a close similarity. From the age of five, Paige felt a strange affinity for the pigeons on the rooftops of the old city. While other children played below, she sat among the birds, and they landed on her shoulders without fear. Her father, who once kept pigeons too, watched her with quiet pride. The same affinity ran through both of them. Affinity comes from the Latin for a neighbour sharing your border: things with an affinity sit naturally close together. So, what word means a natural pull toward something? ... Affinity.

gre.s: Despite growing up in different countries, the two composers shared a striking ____, and critics often mistook one's music for the other's.
gre.clue: critics often mistook one's music for the other's

example: Growing up beside the Padma gave the painter a deep affinity for rivers, which appear in almost every canvas she has made.

en: Appropriate or suitable; having a tendency; quick to learn
hook: APT: APpropriaTe. Also, APTitude for learning.
story: Apt. Suitable for the situation; also, likely to do something, or quick to learn. The new puppy at Logan's house chewed everything: shoes, cushions, and above all, slippers. Within a week the family had named him Slipper. [laugh] Everyone agreed it was an apt name. He was also an apt pupil: in two days he learned to sit for a biscuit. Apt shares its Latin root with aptitude, meaning fitted: an apt word fits the situation perfectly. So, what word describes a name that suits its owner exactly? ... Apt.

gre.s: The critic's description of the novel as a maze was ____, for readers frequently lost track of which narrator was speaking.
gre.clue: for readers frequently lost track

example: Calling the old library the brain of the university was an apt metaphor, since every important idea on campus seemed to start there.

en: To tolerate or allow (usually used in the negative)
hook: GRE trick: BROOK isn't just a stream. 'She brooks no nonsense' means she TOLERATES none.
story: Brook. To tolerate or allow, usually used with no or not. At Lauren's family table, her grandmother brooks no waste. Not a single grain of rice may be left on a plate. She grew up in hard years, when rice was precious, and she still remembers the hunger. When Lauren's cousin once pushed his plate away half full, one look from her was enough. She would not brook it. This brook is not a stream: it almost always comes with no, as in she brooks no excuses. So, what verb means to tolerate, usually in the negative? ... Brook.

gre.s: The editor was famous for her exacting standards and would ____ no errors, however minor, in the articles she approved.
gre.clue: famous for her exacting standards

example: The new captain would brook no complaints about early morning training, and he was always first on the field at six.

en: Logical and consistent; clear and easy to understand
hook: CO-HERENT: all parts ADHERE together.
story: Coherent. Logical and consistent; clear and easy to follow. At three in the morning, Tommy's mother shook him awake to ask where he had put the house keys. Tommy mumbled something about cricket and mangoes, then fell straight back to sleep. Nothing he said was coherent. At breakfast, fully awake, he gave a perfectly coherent answer: the keys were in his jeans pocket. His mother [chuckle] just shook her head. Coherent shares its Latin root with adhere, to stick: in a coherent answer, all the parts stick together. So, what word describes speech that is logical and clear? ... Coherent.

gre.s: The committee's report, written hastily by six authors with conflicting views, failed to present a ____ argument; its chapters frequently contradicted one another.
gre.clue: its chapters frequently contradicted one another

example: After the accident, the shaken bus driver could not give a coherent account of what had happened, so the police waited until morning.

en: The feeling that someone or something is worthless or beneath consideration
hook: CONTEMPT: CON + TEMPT; you're not even tempted to respect it.
story: Contempt. The feeling that someone is worthless or beneath you. At a smart restaurant downtown, a man snapped his fingers at the young waiter, Jamie, and called him stupid for bringing the wrong drink. His voice dripped with contempt. Jamie said nothing. He simply brought the right drink, served the next table with a warm smile, and kept his dignity. Watching, the other diners felt only contempt for the man, not the waiter. In law, contempt of court means treating a judge with open disrespect. So, what word means looking down on someone as worthless? ... Contempt.

gre.s: Far from offering measured criticism, the reviewer made no attempt to hide her ____ for the film, dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph.
gre.clue: dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph

example: The old chess master treated quick online games with open contempt, calling them a noisy kind of gambling.

en: Copied or imitated from others; not original
hook: DERIVATIVE: DERIVED from someone else's work.
story: Derivative. Copied or imitated from others; not original. Cody's band played their first song at a university concert. Friends cheered, but afterwards, an old music teacher said gently, "It sounds like three famous songs stitched together." Cody's face burned. He knew it was true. The song was derivative. So he went home, picked up his guitar, and wrote about his own village and his own mother. That song was nothing but his. Derivative comes from derive: a derivative work is derived from someone else's. So, what word describes art that copies others? ... Derivative.

gre.s: Although the young composer's early works were largely ____, borrowing heavily from his teachers, his later symphonies are startlingly original.
gre.clue: borrowing heavily from his teachers

example: Most of the new cafés in Banani feel derivative, each one copying the same exposed brick, hanging bulbs and avocado toast.

en: Drawn from what is actually observed or tested, not from theory alone
hook: EMPIRICAL: built on EXPERIENCE and EXPERIMENT, like an EMPIRE built brick by brick.
story: Empirical. Based on what is actually observed or tested, not on theory alone. Megan's father believed his old fertiliser was the best, because his own father had used it. Megan, an agriculture student, did not argue. She divided one field into two halves, used the old fertiliser on one side and a new one on the other, and weighed every sack of rice at harvest. Her empirical test settled it. Empirical comes from the Greek for experience: empirical knowledge is gained by seeing and testing. So, what word describes evidence gathered by observation and experiment? ... Empirical.

gre.s: Although the theory was elegant, it lacked ____ support; no one had ever observed the predicted particle in an actual experiment.
gre.clue: no one had ever observed the predicted particle in an actual experiment

example: The economist's claim was finally tested empirically when researchers tracked the spending of two thousand families over five years.

en: Possible and practical to do
hook: FEASIBLE: is it EASY-ble? If it can be done, it's feasible.
story: Feasible. Possible and practical to do. Holly wanted to cycle to her office downtown instead of sitting in traffic for two hours. Her friends said city roads were impossible for cycling. So, one Friday, she tested a route through quieter lanes and along the edge of a park, timing herself. Forty minutes, door to door. [laugh] It was not only possible; it was feasible, and faster than the bus. Feasible comes from the French for doable: a feasible plan is one you can actually do. So, what word describes a plan that is practical and possible? ... Feasible.

gre.s: Engineers concluded that the bridge, though elegant on paper, was not ____ given the region's budget and the instability of its soil.
gre.clue: given the region's budget and the instability of its soil

example: Digging a metro tunnel beneath the narrow lanes of Old Dhaka may not be feasible, so planners are also studying an elevated route.

en: Likely to happen very soon; close at hand
hook: IMMINENT: IN a MINute it will happen.
story: Imminent. About to happen very soon. One April afternoon, the sky over Jenny's village turned the colour of a bruise. The air went still, the birds fell silent, and the smell of dust rose from the fields. A summer storm was imminent. Jenny's mother ran to pull the clothes off the line, shouting for the children to bring in the goats. Minutes later, the wind came roaring. Imminent means hanging over you, ready to fall; do not confuse it with eminent, which means famous. So, what word describes a storm about to break any moment? ... Imminent.

gre.s: Although officials insisted there was no cause for alarm, residents could see that the dam's collapse was ____, as water was already spilling over its cracked walls.
gre.clue: water was already spilling over its cracked walls

example: With the monsoon imminent, farmers in Bogura worked late into the night to bring in the last of the boro rice.

en: Of vital importance; essential
hook: IMPERATIVE: an IMPERIAL command, must be done.
story: Imperative. Of vital importance; absolutely essential. When Lucas's high fever turned out to be dengue, the doctor was very clear with his parents. It was imperative that he drink fluids every hour, rest completely, and come back at once if his gums bled. His mother set an alarm and sat by his bed with oral saline through the night. Imperative comes from the same root as emperor and imperial: an imperative is like an emperor's command, which must be obeyed. So, what word describes something absolutely necessary that cannot be ignored? ... Imperative.

gre.s: With the river rising by the hour, the engineers considered it ____ that the embankment be reinforced before nightfall; any delay could flood the entire district.
gre.clue: any delay could flood the entire district

example: For astronauts on long missions, daily exercise is imperative, since muscles and bones weaken quickly without gravity.

en: A formal charge of a serious crime; a strong criticism
hook: INDICTMENT (in-DITE-ment): the court DICTATES charges.
story: Indictment. A formal charge of a serious crime; also, a strong criticism. After just twenty minutes of rain, a main road in the city turned into a brown river. Victor took a photo: a rickshaw puller wading through water up to his waist, pulling a schoolgirl holding her bag above her head. The photo spread everywhere. People called it an indictment of the city's drainage. Indictment hides a silent c, and it shares a root with dictate: an indictment speaks the charge aloud. So, what word means a strong condemnation, or a formal criminal charge? ... Indictment.

gre.s: The report was a damning ____ of the agency's leadership, detailing years of ignored warnings, falsified data, and entirely preventable deaths.
gre.clue: detailing years of ignored warnings

example: The empty classrooms in the new school were a silent indictment of the officials who had spent the teachers' salaries on decorations.

en: Spreading harmfully into new areas; intrusive
hook: INVASIVE: INVADES and takes over.
story: Invasive. Spreading harmfully into new areas; also, intrusive. Abby's grandfather remembers when the village pond was clear enough to see the fish. Then a few plants of water hyacinth floated in. Within two summers, the thick green carpet covered every inch, blocking sunlight and choking the fish below. Water hyacinth first came from South America, and in the delta it is one of the most invasive plants of all. Invasive comes from invade: an invasive plant invades and takes over. So, what word describes something that spreads harmfully into new places? ... Invasive.

gre.s: Ecologists warn that the ____ beetle, introduced accidentally through shipping crates, threatens to wipe out the region's native oaks.
gre.clue: introduced accidentally through shipping crates

example: Lionfish, an invasive species in the Caribbean, eat so many young reef fish that divers are now encouraged to spear them.

en: Clearly evident (adj.); to show or display (verb)
hook: MANIFEST: so obvious it's in your hand (manus).
story: Manifest. Clearly visible and obvious; as a verb, to show or display. Little Max's love of numbers manifested early. At four, he counted every stair in his building. At six, he added up the grocery bill faster than the shopkeeper, who [chuckle] gave him a free toffee for it. By his tenth birthday, his gift was manifest to everyone who met him. Think of a ship's manifest, the list that makes every piece of cargo plain to see. So, what word describes something clear and obvious to everyone? ... Manifest.

gre.s: Although the director insisted the project was on schedule, its failure was ____ to everyone else: half the buildings stood unfinished and the funds were gone.
gre.clue: half the buildings stood unfinished and the funds were gone

example: Her talent for languages was manifest by the age of six, when she was chatting with tourists in English, Hindi and Arabic.

en: No longer in use; out of date
hook: OBSOLETE: 'OBviously SOLD long ago', not sold anymore.
story: Obsolete. No longer in use; out of date. Clearing out his grandfather's cupboard, Sean found a shoebox of cassette tapes, a tangle of brown ribbon, and an old Walkman with no batteries. He held one up and asked what it was. His grandfather laughed and told him how he once rewound tapes with a pencil to save the batteries. To Sean, it all looked obsolete, like objects from a museum. Obsolete comes from a Latin verb meaning to wear out with age. So, what word describes technology that nobody uses anymore? ... Obsolete.

gre.s: Within a decade of its introduction, the once-revolutionary device had become ____, displaced by smaller and cheaper alternatives.
gre.clue: displaced by smaller and cheaper alternatives

example: Mobile banking has made the old postal money order nearly obsolete, even in the most remote villages of Bangladesh.

en: Strange or unusual; belonging exclusively to one person or place
hook: PECULIAR: PECULIAR things are PECULIARLY yours.
story: Peculiar. Strange or unusual; also, belonging only to one place or person. When Kelsey first tasted beef cooked with a wild hill lemon at her friend's home in the hills, she paused. The flavour was peculiar: sour, slightly bitter, and wonderfully fragrant all at once. Her friend explained that the fruit, a large bitter citrus, grows mainly in that one region. The dish is peculiar to those hills. Peculiar first meant one's own private property in Latin, so something peculiar belongs to one place alone. So, what word describes something strange, or special to one place only? ... Peculiar.

gre.s: The custom of exchanging salt as a gift is ____ to the region and is unknown even in neighboring provinces.
gre.clue: unknown even in neighboring provinces

example: The sharp smell of drying fish is peculiar to the shutki yards of Cox's Bazar, and visitors notice it long before they see the racks.

en: Ordinary and dull, with no spark or imagination
hook: GRE trick: PEDESTRIAN = as dull as plodding along on foot.
story: Pedestrian. Ordinary and dull, with no imagination. Rachel's first essay on her favourite season began, "The year has four seasons. Winter is cold. Winter is nice." Her teacher wrote one word in the margin: pedestrian. So Rachel tried again. She wrote about fog on the pond, steam rising from her mother's rice cakes, and her grandfather's shawl smelling of mustard oil. This time the teacher wrote: beautiful. Ped means foot, as in pedal; a pedestrian walks, and pedestrian writing plods along instead of flying. So, what word describes writing that is dull and unimaginative? ... Pedestrian.

gre.s: Although the film's special effects were dazzling, its plot was disappointingly ____, recycling clichés that audiences had seen countless times before.
gre.clue: recycling clichés that audiences had seen countless times before

example: Her translation was accurate but pedestrian, turning the poet's playful lines into the flat language of a government notice.

en: Of minor importance; on the edge or outer part
hook: PERIPHERAL: on the PERIMETER, at the edge.
story: Peripheral. Of minor importance; also, on the outer edge. Dylan spent his first GRE week making the perfect study space. He bought coloured pens, designed a timetable, decorated his notebook, and arranged his desk lamp just right. On Friday he realised he had not solved a single question. [sigh] All of it had been peripheral, while the real work sat waiting at the centre. Peripheral comes from the Greek for around, the same peri as in perimeter, the outer edge. So, what word describes things at the edge, not at the heart of the matter? ... Peripheral.

gre.s: The committee dismissed the objection as ____, since it concerned the project's color scheme rather than its safety or cost.
gre.clue: rather than its safety or cost

example: In the court case, the question of who owned the car was peripheral, since the only real issue was who had been driving it.

en: Reasonable enough that it might well be true
hook: PLAUSIBLE: deserves APPLAUSE for sounding right.
story: Plausible. Reasonable enough that it might be true. Nick had not finished his assignment. He told his professor that a power cut had lasted all evening and his laptop battery had died. In the city, during a hot summer, that was perfectly plausible, and the professor gave him one more day. But when his classmate claimed a goat had eaten his pen drive, the professor laughed out loud. That excuse was far less plausible. Plausible comes from the Latin for deserving applause: a plausible story sounds good enough to applaud. So, what word describes an explanation that seems believable? ... Plausible.

gre.s: Although the detective's theory was ____ enough to persuade the jury, later DNA evidence showed that the actual sequence of events had been quite different.
gre.clue: enough to persuade the jury

example: Many scientists find it plausible that comets carried water to the young Earth, though the evidence is still debated.

en: Producing a strong effect; very powerful
hook: POTENT: full of POTENTIAL power.
story: Potent. Very powerful; having a strong effect. At a family picnic in the hills, Jay's cousins dared him to bite into a naga chilli straight from the garden. He [chuckle] took a big bite. [gasp] Seconds later his face turned red, tears streamed from his eyes, and he gulped down a whole jug of water. The naga chilli is among the most potent chillies in the world. Potent shares its root with potential: both are about power. So, what word describes something with a very strong effect? ... Potent.

gre.s: Though the drug is administered in tiny doses, it is remarkably ____: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse.
gre.clue: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse

example: A single photograph of a cracked riverbed became a potent symbol of the drought, printed on posters across the country.

en: A person authorized to act for another; a substitute
hook: PROXY: like a PROXY attendance a friend gives for you in class.
story: Proxy. A person authorised to act for someone else; a substitute. In a big lecture hall, the teacher called the roll. When she said "Steve," a voice from the back called out "Present," though Steve was home asleep. His friend was his proxy. The teacher looked up, [chuckle] smiled, and called Steve's number again, staring straight at the friend. Students call this giving proxy: answering in someone else's place. So, what word means a person who stands in for someone else? ... Proxy.

gre.s: Since thermometers did not exist in the Middle Ages, climatologists use the width of tree rings as a ____ for direct temperature records from that period.
gre.clue: Since thermometers did not exist in the Middle Ages

example: Economists often use satellite images of city lights at night as a proxy for economic activity in countries with poor statistics.

en: Enforced separation to stop a disease spreading; to separate in this way
hook: QUARANTINE: from Italian 'quaranta', forty days of isolation for ships.
story: Quarantine. Forced separation to stop a disease from spreading; as a verb, to separate in this way. When Mark flew home from abroad during a dangerous outbreak, he spent two weeks in quarantine in a single room of his house. His daughter could not hug him, so every evening she pressed a drawing against the window glass, and he pressed his hand against it from inside. The word comes from the Italian for forty: in old Venice, ships from plague ports had to wait forty days before landing. So, what word means isolation to stop a disease spreading? ... Quarantine.

gre.s: Health officials decided to ____ the entire village after the outbreak, barring anyone from leaving until tests confirmed that the virus was no longer spreading.
gre.clue: barring anyone from leaving

example: New fish should be quarantined in a separate tank for two weeks before they join the others in the main aquarium.

en: To forcibly stop; to prevent from being expressed
hook: SUP-PRESS: PRESS it down.
story: Suppress. To forcibly stop something; to hold back a feeling. During the school's morning assembly, the headmaster was giving a very serious speech. Then a pigeon landed on his head and calmly sat there. Five hundred students bit their lips, stared at their shoes and tried to suppress their laughter. Ellie pressed both hands over her mouth, [chuckle] but a tiny sound escaped. She could not suppress it. Suppress means to press down, from the Latin for pressing under: you press a feeling down until it stays hidden. So, what verb means to hold something back by force? ... Suppress.

gre.s: Though the regime tried to ____ news of the protests, reports spread quickly through encrypted messaging apps beyond the reach of state censors.
gre.clue: beyond the reach of state censors

example: The company tried to suppress the safety report, but one of its engineers leaked it to a journalist in Khulna.

en: Able to be touched; clear and definite, real
hook: TANGIBLE: you can TOUCH it (tangere = to touch).
story: Tangible. Able to be touched; real and definite. For a year, Erin's online fundraiser for a flooded village school was only numbers on a screen. Some days, she wondered if any of it mattered. Then she visited. A new tin roof shone in the sun, children sat at new desks, and books lay dry on the shelves. She ran her hand along a desk. The result was tangible at last. Tangible comes from the Latin for touch, as in tangent, a line that touches a circle. So, what word describes results you can see and touch? ... Tangible.

gre.s: Despite years of lofty promises about reform, the government had produced few ____ improvements that ordinary citizens could actually see in their daily lives.
gre.clue: that ordinary citizens could actually see in their daily lives

example: After six months of tutoring, the children's reading scores showed tangible progress, and two of them won places at the district school.

en: Relating to worldly as opposed to spiritual matters; relating to time
hook: TEMPORAL: TEMPORARY earthly things versus eternal spiritual ones.
story: Temporal. Relating to worldly life rather than spiritual matters; also, relating to time. At a riverside fair, an old folk singer sat with his one-string lute under a banyan tree. Houses, money and fame, he sang, are temporal; they fade like footprints on the riverbank. Only the soul remains. Jordan, who had come to sell phones, stopped and listened until the song ended. Temporal comes from the Latin tempus, time, as in temporary: temporal things belong to this passing time. So, what word describes worldly matters rather than spiritual ones? ... Temporal.

gre.s: The medieval church claimed authority not only over spiritual life but also over ____ affairs, collecting taxes and settling property disputes like any secular ruler.
gre.clue: collecting taxes and settling property disputes like any secular ruler

example: Many Sufi teachers urged their followers to look beyond temporal rewards such as wealth and fame toward a life of the spirit.

en: Too small or unimportant to matter much
hook: TRIVIAL: like TRIVIA, small unimportant facts.
story: Trivial. Too small or unimportant to matter. Katie and her sister Lisa stopped speaking for three whole weeks. The reason? Who had eaten the last piece of fish at dinner. Their mother pleaded, their father sighed, and the house felt cold. Finally, Katie bought two plates of street snacks and knocked on Lisa's door. They both [laugh] wondered how such a trivial fight had lasted so long. Trivial shares its root with trivia: small, unimportant facts. So, what word describes a problem too small to matter? ... Trivial.

gre.s: Although the error seemed ____ at the time, a mere decimal point out of place, it eventually cost the company millions.
gre.clue: it eventually cost the company millions

example: The two ministers quarrelled over trivial details of the seating plan while the flood relief budget went undiscussed.

en: To weaken something gradually or secretly
hook: UNDER-MINE: digging a MINE UNDER a wall until it collapses.
story: Undermine. To weaken something gradually or secretly. Every monsoon, the great river eats quietly away at the soil beneath its banks. From above, the land in Hank's village looks solid, green with jute. But below, the river is hollowing it out. One morning, a whole strip of field cracks and slides into the water. The river had undermined it for months. The word began in war: soldiers dug mines under castle walls until the walls fell. So, what verb means to weaken something from beneath, slowly or secretly? ... Undermine.

gre.s: Critics warned that the new law would ____ judicial independence by allowing politicians to dismiss judges at will.
gre.clue: by allowing politicians to dismiss judges at will

example: Constant rumors that the coach would be sacked undermined the players' confidence throughout the second half of the season.

en: Able to do many different things well
hook: VERSATILE: works in every VERSE, every situation.
story: Versatile. Able to do many different things well. Amber's aunt Diane teaches maths at a village school. On weekends, she repairs neighbours' sewing machines, cooks for every family wedding, and coaches the girls' football team. When the school's harmonium player fell ill before a concert, Diane sat down and played it herself. Everyone agreed she was the most versatile person they knew. Versatile comes from the Latin for turning, as in reverse: a versatile person turns easily from one task to another. So, what word describes someone skilled at many different things? ... Versatile.

gre.s: The ____ actor, equally convincing as a villain, a comic sidekick, or a tragic hero, has worked in nearly every genre.
gre.clue: equally convincing as a villain, a comic sidekick, or a tragic hero

example: Jute is a versatile fiber, woven into sacks and carpets, pressed into car panels, and even blended into fashionable shirts.

en: Likely to change suddenly and without warning, often for the worse
hook: VOLATILE: like a VOLCANO, could explode any moment.
story: Volatile. Likely to change suddenly and without warning, often for the worse. Gary sells onions at a town market. One week, a kilo is cheap. The next, after news of a bad harvest or a border closure, the price jumps two or three times overnight. Customers shout, and Gary shrugs helplessly. Onion prices there are famously volatile. Volatile comes from the Latin for flying: a volatile liquid like petrol flies off into the air, and volatile prices fly up without warning. So, what word describes something that can change suddenly and wildly? ... Volatile.

gre.s: Investors fled the ____ market, where prices could swing by double digits in a single afternoon.
gre.clue: where prices could swing by double digits in a single afternoon

example: The mood in the dressing room was volatile after the defeat, so the captain waited until morning to discuss what had gone wrong.

en: Very tired; also, having lost patience with something
hook: WEARY: worn out from WEARING the same burden too long.
story: Weary. Very tired; also, tired of something and out of patience. Two days before the holiday, Tina spent eight hours in the crowds of the big market, bargaining for a dress, shoes and bangles. By evening her feet ached, her voice was hoarse, and she was weary of bargaining. On the bus home, she leaned her head on the window, [sigh] utterly weary, but holding her shopping bags tight. Do not confuse weary with wary: weary means worn out, wary means cautious. So, what word describes someone tired out after a long, hard day? ... Weary.

gre.s: After a decade of conflict, the population had grown ____ of war and overwhelmingly supported the peace agreement.
gre.clue: overwhelmingly supported the peace agreement

example: Readers had grown weary of the columnist's weekly complaints about traffic, and many of them simply skipped her page.

en: To hold up against something without being harmed
hook: WITH-STAND: STAND firm against.
story: Withstand. To hold up against something without being harmed. When Roy built his new house near the coast, he raised it on strong concrete pillars and tied the roof down with steel. Neighbours thought he was overdoing it. Then a cyclone struck. Trees fell, and tin roofs flew across the fields, but Roy's house withstood the storm, and his neighbours sheltered inside. In old English, with meant against, so to withstand is to stand against. So, what verb means to resist a force without breaking? ... Withstand.

gre.s: Unlike the flimsy bridges that collapsed during the flood, the new suspension bridge was engineered to ____ even the most violent currents.
gre.clue: Unlike the flimsy bridges that collapsed during the flood

example: Though it lost its nine spires in an earthquake, the Kantajew temple continues to withstand the monsoon rains, as it has for nearly three centuries.
